extracted.intended_audience: general readers and media/television students or practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and describe the features, formats, and related subgenres of the television/radio/theatrical variety show genre across regions and eras. Useful for distinguishing types of variety programming and their characteristic elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core definition: variety of acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Variety show, also known as variety arts or variety entertainment, is entertainment made up of a variety of acts including musical performances, sketch comedy, magic, acrobatics, juggling, and ventriloquism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the defining dimension: a program should present multiple, distinct performance types rather than a single-genre show. Examples cited include musical performances and sketch comedy; anti-patterns would be single-genre programs that lack multiple act types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of a compère/host
rubrics_metrics.description: It is normally introduced by a compère (master of ceremonies) or host.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many classic and modern variety shows rely on a single host or compère to introduce acts and provide continuity. Exceptions include ensemble sketch shows that use rotating guest hosts (e.g., SNL) or no single lead host.

rubrics_metrics.name: Radio-era components: house vocalist, house band, monologue, comedy sketch
rubrics_metrics.description: Radio variety shows typically included a house vocalist, music from the house band, a stand-up monologue and a short comedy sketch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adapting to audio-first media, evaluate inclusion of these elements as characteristic of traditional radio-style variety programming (e.g., Golden Age of Radio). These components influenced early TV variety structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recurring sketches/characters and their evolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Variety shows centered on running comedy sketches with recurring characters eventually evolved into sitcoms (situation comedies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A variety show's use of recurring characters/sketches can be judged as a strength (building audience familiarity) or as a seed for spin-off formats (sitcoms). Lack of recurring material may make a show feel less coherent across episodes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Segmented structure with themed recurring segments
rubrics_metrics.description: Many variety programs are structured around recurring themed segments — e.g., a large dance party showcasing a new dance, celebrity guest and dozens of professional dancers (The Arthur Murray Party).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective variety shows often mix dependable recurring segments (dance, guest performances, comedy bits) with novelty acts. Overreliance on one segment type can reduce perceived variety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live or live-like presentation and audience interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically many variety shows were performed live (stage, radio, early television) and featured live audience elements (e.g., Royal Variety Performance); some contemporary shows retain a live-like, fast-paced presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Live presentation influences pacing, spontaneity, and audience engagement. Modern productions may simulate 'live' energy even when pre-recorded; failure to convey immediacy can make a variety show feel flat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration with talk-show/interview elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Late-night talk shows combine variety entertainment (comedy and live music) with talk-show aspects such as interviews; the two genres have been closely related.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A program blending interviews, sketches, and music fits within the variety family; assess balance — too much interview content shifts it toward talk show territory, too little makes it less of a hybrid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Host model distinction: single lead host vs guest-host/ensemble
rubrics_metrics.description: Some variety formats are built around a single lead host (traditional variety), while sketch-comedy series may lack a single lead host and instead use different guest hosts or an ensemble cast (e.g., SNL).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether the show’s identity relies on a consistent host persona or on ensemble/guest hosts; this affects continuity, branding, and audience expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Talent-show / competition elements as variety components
rubrics_metrics.description: Televised talent shows feature a variety show element by presenting a diversity of acts (e.g., Star Search, The Gong Show, Got Talent franchise).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a talent-competition, consider whether variety is achieved via breadth of disciplines and presentation style. Competitive scoring mechanisms differentiate these from non-competitive variety programming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telethon format: entertainment interspersed with fundraising appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: The variety show format continued in the telethon, which features variety entertainment (often music) interspersed with appeals for donations to support a charity or cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments should account for the dual aims (entertainment + fundraising). Pacing and placement of donation appeals are key to balancing audience retention and fundraising goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional stylistic conventions — East Asian shows (sound effects, on-screen visuals, banter)
rubrics_metrics.description: East Asian variety programs (Taiwan, Japan, Korea) are noted for constant use of sound effects, on-screen visuals (telop), comedic bantering, fast-paced live-like presentation, and sometimes repetition or fast-forwarding of scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or producing shows aimed at East Asian markets or influenced by them, emphasize visual on-screen elements and brisk editing; Western-style pacing may not translate. Specific features (telop) are cultural stylistic markers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Korean 'Real Variety Show' model: unscripted stunts and location-based settings
rubrics_metrics.description: Korean programs like Infinite Challenge introduced a 'Real Variety Show' model combining comedy and variety scenes including unscripted stunts and special guest stars while taking place in various settings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value is placed on spontaneity, challenge-driven formats, and varied locations. Over-scripting undermines the 'real' quality; safety and logistics are important when staging unscripted stunts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specials format: celebrity-hosted themed specials (e.g., Christmas shows)
rubrics_metrics.description: Christmas and other variety specials often show the star in a set meant to look like their home, welcoming singers and other guests to perform duets of Christmas songs; many entertainers became associated with recurring specials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specials emphasize theme, star image, and repeatable annual formats. Evaluate consistency of theme, guest selection, and production values; these specials can outlast weekly formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hybridization with other genres (tabloid talk, cooking, talent, sketch)
rubrics_metrics.description: Variety shows are often combined with elements of other genres — e.g., talk shows incorporating music and games, cooking elements, talent competitions, or tabloid talk with absurdist games (Richard Bey Show).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hybrid formats should be judged on coherence of the blend. Poor integration (e.g., abrupt genre shifts, tonal clashes) is an anti-pattern; successful hybrids create a consistent viewer experience despite mixed elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exportability and syndication / longevity markers
rubrics_metrics.description: Many long-running variety shows (e.g., The Ed Sullivan Show, Programa Silvio Santos, Sabado Gigante) became cultural institutions and were often exported or syndicated; longevity can reflect broad appeal and adaptability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure success partly by run length, syndication/export potential, and cultural impact. However, long runs can also indicate format stasis; consider renewal of segments and talent to maintain relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation across media and eras (stage → radio → television → digital)
rubrics_metrics.description: The variety format moved from Victorian-era stage music hall and vaudeville to radio and then television, and later adapted (or declined) under multichannel television and digital fragmentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating/evaluating a variety program, consider medium-specific constraints and opportunities (visuals for TV, audio pacing for radio, discoverability on digital platforms). Failure to adapt to medium/audience fragmentation reduces viability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety and ethical considerations for large-audience segments
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples such as crowd crushes (Wowowee) and controversies over rigged game segments highlight safety and fairness issues in large live-audience or mass-participation segments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers must prioritize crowd management, transparent game mechanics, and ethical conduct. Incidents of harm or perceived rigging are severe anti-patterns that can end shows or provoke legal consequences.
